text: Lesson 7 showed how to create arrays and do math on them. This lesson covers two skills you'll use in every analysis: selecting the part of an array you need, and combining arrays of different shapes without writing loops. Selection uses indexing and slicing. Combining uses a NumPy rule called broadcasting.

Indexing works like Python lists — positions start at 0, negative positions count from the end, and a slice start-colon-stop-colon-step includes start and stops just before stop. On a five-price array, position 0 is 20, position negative 1 is 42. Slicing 1 to 4 gives three middle values. Stepping by 2 gives every other value, and a step of negative 1 reverses the whole array.

Unlike plain lists, NumPy also lets you index with a list of positions, which picks exactly those elements in that order. Indexing prices with the list 0, 2, 4 gives you those three values back, in that order — something a plain Python list can't do directly.

Here's the most common surprise for newcomers: a basic slice does not copy the data — it gives you a window onto the same memory. Slice out positions 1 through 3, change its first element to 99, and the original array changes too — the price 55.5 got silently overwritten through the slice. When you want an independent array, call dot-copy instead; then changes to the copy leave the original untouched. Rule of thumb: copy when you plan to modify a selection and need the original safe.

For a 2D array you give one index per dimension, rows first, separated by a comma, and a bare colon means everything along that dimension. Build a 3 by 4 array, and m at row 1, column 2 gives you 6. m at row 0 alone gives the whole first row. m with a colon for rows and column 1 gives the second column down every row. And m sliced 0 to 2 by 1 to 3 pulls out a 2 by 2 block. Think of it as m of rows, columns — pandas uses this exact mental model in Chapter 3.

Boolean masks work on 2D arrays too, returning a flat array of just the matching values — m where m is greater than 8 gives you 9, 10, 11. And a mask can assign, not just select: set every negative value in an array to zero in one line, a with a less-than-zero equals zero. That's a common, one-line cleaning step you'll reuse constantly.

What happens when you multiply a 2D array by a 1D array? Say orders holds quantities for two customers across three products, shape 2 by 3, and unit holds the price of each product, shape 3. Multiplying them gives you each customer's cost per product, because NumPy stretches the smaller array across the larger one without actually copying it. The rule: compare shapes from the rightmost dimension backward — two dimensions are compatible if they're equal or one of them is 1.

A column of shape 2 by 1 stretches along the columns instead — adding it to the unit-price array broadcasts out to a full 2 by 3 result. A real use of this: centering each column of a dataset by subtracting its mean along axis 0, turning raw values into deviations from the average in a single line — no loop required.

If shapes aren't compatible, NumPy raises an error rather than guessing. Add a shape-2 array directly to the 2-by-3 orders array, and you get a ValueError, because the last dimensions, 3 and 2, don't match. The fix: reshape bad into a column with bad, colon, comma, None — giving it shape 2 by 1 — and now it broadcasts one value per row correctly.

To recap: index with a single bracket, slice with start-stop-step, and use rows-comma-columns in 2D. Basic slices are views — call dot-copy when you need independence. Lists of positions and boolean masks select elements and can assign values. Broadcasting compares shapes from the right, and dimensions must match or be 1.
